quests.q: What does the "MFA fatigue" attack rely on — a user doing what?
quests.hint: The attacker already has the password; they spam login attempts until the victim taps the wrong button.
quests.explain: Attackers flood a victim with push notifications until they approve one just to stop the noise. Fix: number-matching MFA.

quests.q: Name the 2023–24 supply-chain backdoor planted in a Linux compression library, referred to by the package name.
quests.hint: A maintainer social-engineered their way to commit access over 2 years, then hid an sshd backdoor in the build.
quests.explain: CVE-2024-3094: a backdoor in xz/liblzma nearly reached every major distro. Caught by a Postgres dev noticing 500ms of latency.

quests.q: What OWASP category tops the LLM Top 10 — injecting malicious instructions into a model's input?
quests.hint: It is #1 on the OWASP Top 10 for LLM apps, direct or indirect.
quests.explain: Prompt injection (LLM01) smuggles attacker instructions into the prompt — e.g. hidden text on a web page an agent reads.

quests.q: What class of cryptography is being standardized to survive quantum computers — the "PQC" in NIST's 2024 standards?
quests.hint: NIST finalized ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA in Aug 2024.
quests.explain: Post-quantum cryptography resists Shor's algorithm. FIPS 203/204/205 standardized lattice- and hash-based schemes.

quests.q: In "zero trust", what is the core assumption about the network?
quests.hint: The motto is a four-word phrase about trust and verification.
quests.explain: Zero trust assumes breach: no implicit trust from network location; every request is authenticated and authorized.

quests.q: What is it called when an attacker abuses an over-permissioned OAuth token instead of a password — the token being a stolen what?
quests.hint: These bypass MFA entirely because the auth already happened; also called token/cookie theft.
quests.explain: Stolen session tokens (e.g. via infostealers) replay an authenticated session, sidestepping password + MFA. Bind tokens to device.

quests.q: What kind of malware encrypts files and demands payment?
quests.hint: Ransom + software.
quests.explain: Ransomware encrypts victim data and extorts payment; modern strains also exfiltrate first for "double extortion".

quests.q: What technique hides malicious instructions inside content an AI agent will later read — e.g. white text on a web page?
quests.hint: It is "indirect" because the payload isn't typed by the user — the model fetches it.
quests.explain: Indirect prompt injection plants instructions in data the LLM ingests (pages, emails, docs), hijacking agents that browse.

quests.q: SIM-swapping attacks defeat which specific weak form of MFA?
quests.hint: The attacker ports your phone number to their SIM to intercept these codes.
quests.explain: SMS-based OTPs are phishable and interceptable via SIM swap. Prefer authenticator apps or FIDO2 hardware keys.

quests.q: What is the name of the phishing-resistant, hardware-backed authentication standard using public-key crypto, branded "passkeys"?
quests.hint: The W3C API side is WebAuthn; the alliance spec is this.
quests.explain: FIDO2 (WebAuthn + CTAP) uses device-bound key pairs — nothing phishable is ever sent. Passkeys are the consumer branding.

quests.q: What do you call a security flaw with zero days of vendor warning and no patch available?
quests.hint: The name is a number plus "day".
quests.explain: A zero-day is exploited before a fix exists. Defense leans on behavior detection and exposure reduction, not patching.

quests.q: In cloud security, what misconfiguration exposed the most breaches — a storage container set to what access?
quests.hint: Think S3 buckets left open to the internet.
quests.explain: Publicly-readable object storage (S3, GCS, Blob) remains a top breach cause. Enforce block-public-access org-wide.

quests.q: A deepfake used to impersonate a CEO on a video call to authorize a transfer is an example of what social-engineering goal?
quests.hint: The end goal is stealing money through deception.
quests.explain: A 2024 Arup case saw $25M wired after a deepfaked video call. Verify high-value requests out-of-band, always.

quests.q: What attack poisons an ML model by tampering with its training data — the "poisoning" happening at which phase?
quests.hint: Contrast with an evasion attack, which happens at inference time.
quests.explain: Data-poisoning corrupts the training set to plant backdoors or degrade accuracy. MITRE ATLAS catalogs such ML attacks.

quests.q: What does the "principle of least privilege" tell you to grant?
quests.hint: Give only the minimum access needed for the job.
quests.explain: Least privilege limits blast radius: users/services get only the permissions their task requires, nothing spare.

quests.q: What is the term for an attacker moving from one compromised host to others inside the network?
quests.hint: Two words: sideways + motion.
quests.explain: Lateral movement is post-compromise spread across hosts. Segmentation + least privilege + EDR shrink it.

quests.q: CAPTCHAs are designed to distinguish humans from what?
quests.hint: Automated scripts.
quests.explain: CAPTCHAs gate automation. Note: you should never build tools to auto-solve them for others — that's abuse.

quests.q: Which framework catalogs real-world adversary tactics and techniques by ID (e.g. T1566 phishing)?
quests.hint: MITRE + a four-letter acronym meaning "attack".
quests.explain: MITRE ATT&CK maps tactics→techniques observed in the wild; blue teams use it to measure detection coverage.

quests.q: What is a "honeypot" in security?
quests.hint: A deliberate trap that looks like a real target.
quests.explain: A honeypot is a decoy system that lures and studies attackers, generating high-signal alerts with near-zero false positives.

quests.q: The 2024 "regreSSHion" bug (CVE-2024-6387) was a remote unauthenticated flaw in which widely-deployed daemon?
quests.hint: The name puns on regression + the protocol it implements.
quests.explain: regreSSHion was a race condition in OpenSSH's sshd giving potential RCE as root on glibc Linux. Patch to 9.8p1+.

quests.q: What does encrypting data "in transit" protect against?
quests.hint: Someone listening on the wire — interception.
quests.explain: TLS encrypts data in transit so on-path attackers can't read or tamper. Pair with encryption at rest.

quests.q: What is the practice of continuously verifying software provenance via signed build attestations, popularized by "SLSA"?
quests.hint: SLSA = Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts.
quests.explain: SLSA raises trust in build pipelines with provenance + signing (e.g. Sigstore), countering xz-style implants.

quests.q: A password manager's main security benefit is enabling passwords that are what?
quests.hint: One different password per site.
quests.explain: Managers make long, unique, random passwords practical — killing credential-stuffing from reused passwords.

quests.q: What cryptographic property ensures a compromised long-term key can't decrypt past captured traffic?
quests.hint: Also called "perfect ___ ___". Ephemeral keys per session.
quests.explain: Forward secrecy (ephemeral DH per session) means stealing the server key later won't decrypt yesterday's recorded TLS.

quests.q: What social-engineering attack uses email to trick you into revealing credentials?
quests.hint: Sounds like a water sport.
quests.explain: Phishing lures victims to fake login pages or malicious attachments. FIDO2 passkeys make it far harder to succeed.

quests.q: In AI red-teaming, what is a "jailbreak"?
quests.hint: Getting a model to ignore its guardrails / restrictions.
quests.explain: A jailbreak crafts inputs that defeat a model's safety training. Defenses: system-prompt hardening, input/output filters, eval suites.

quests.q: Decode this base64 and submit the result: Q3lBcnQ=
quests.hint: Base64 is encoding, not encryption — any decoder (or `atob` in your browser console) reverses it.
quests.explain: Base64 encodes binary as text; it hides nothing. Spotting and decoding it is a daily skill in CTFs and malware triage.

quests.q: Log4Shell was tracked as CVE-2021-_____. Fill in the number.
quests.hint: Search "log4shell CVE" — learning to look up CVEs IS the skill being tested.
quests.explain: CVE-2021-44228 let attackers run code via a log string (${jndi:ldap://…}). One log line = full server takeover. Patch fast, log carefully.

quests.q: A Caesar cipher shifted each letter by 3. Decode: FBEHU
quests.hint: Shift every letter 3 back in the alphabet: F→C…
quests.explain: Caesar is the "hello world" of cryptanalysis — trivial today, but it teaches the core idea: ciphers are reversible transforms.

quests.q: Attackers doing SSRF against cloud servers target one magic IP to steal credentials. Which IP?
quests.hint: It's the link-local metadata endpoint on AWS/GCP/Azure.
quests.explain: The metadata service hands out IAM credentials to the instance. SSRF that reaches 169.254.169.254 = cloud account takeover. Enforce IMDSv2.

quests.q: Which port does HTTPS use by default?
quests.hint: HTTP is 80; secure HTTP is this.
quests.explain: Knowing default ports (22 SSH, 53 DNS, 443 HTTPS) lets you read scan results and firewall rules at a glance.

quests.q: A JWT can sometimes be forged by changing its algorithm header to which value?
quests.hint: The token then claims it needs no signature at all.
quests.explain: The alg:none attack strips signature verification when servers naively trust the header. Always allowlist algorithms server-side.

quests.q: The classic injection payload `' OR 1=1 --` belongs to which attack?
quests.hint: It abuses a database query built from user input.
quests.explain: SQLi lets input rewrite queries. The fix has been known for 20 years: parameterized queries. It still tops breach reports.

quests.q: Which attack cracks Active Directory service-account passwords offline using requested service tickets?
quests.hint: Kerberos + roasting.
quests.explain: Kerberoasting requests SPN tickets encrypted with the service account's password hash, then cracks them offline. Fix: long random passwords, gMSA.

quests.q: What is the "network mapper" tool every security beginner learns for port scanning?
quests.hint: The name literally abbreviates "network mapper".
quests.explain: nmap discovers hosts, open ports, and services. Run it against scanme.nmap.org (explicitly permitted) — never against systems you don't own.

quests.q: XXE is an injection attack abusing XML ______ entities. Fill the blank.
quests.hint: The X-X-E acronym itself contains the answer.
quests.explain: XXE makes an XML parser fetch attacker-chosen files/URLs. Fix: disable external entity resolution — one config line.

quests.q: Phishing that arrives by SMS text message is called what?
quests.hint: SMS + phishing, squished together.
quests.explain: "Your parcel is held, click here" — smishing exploits urgency on small screens. Same defense: never auth via links you didn't request.

quests.q: Heartbleed (2014) leaked server memory from which cryptographic library?
quests.hint: The library behind most of the era's TLS.
quests.explain: Heartbleed read 64KB of server RAM per heartbeat — keys, passwords, sessions. Lesson: a memory-safety bug in one library = internet-wide crisis.

quests.q: Adding a random value to each password before hashing is called what?
quests.hint: Season the password before you cook it.
quests.explain: Salts make identical passwords hash differently, killing rainbow tables. Use a slow KDF like bcrypt or argon2, never a bare hash.

quests.q: The 2024 xz backdoor (CVE-2024-3094) was caught because sshd got about how many hundred milliseconds slower — 500 or 5?
quests.hint: A dev noticed sub-second latency that shouldn't exist.
quests.explain: A Postgres engineer chased a 500ms sshd slowdown and uncovered a near-miss supply-chain implant. Curiosity about anomalies is a security skill.

quests.q: The MITRE framework that maps real adversary techniques by ID (like T1566 for phishing) is called MITRE ______.
quests.hint: Sounds exactly like the word "attack".
quests.explain: Learning to look up a technique on MITRE ATT&CK turns "we got hacked" into a precise, communicable diagnosis. Blue teams live in it.

quests.q: CISA maintains a catalog of vulnerabilities that are being actively exploited right now, abbreviated ____. Four letters.
quests.hint: Known Exploited Vulnerabilities.
quests.explain: The KEV catalog tells you which CVEs attackers actually use — the single best patch-prioritization list on the internet, and it's free.

quests.q: A password like "correcthorsebatterystaple" is strong mainly because of its ____ (how long it is). One word.
quests.hint: More characters beat clever symbols.
quests.explain: Entropy grows with length far faster than with special-character rules. A long passphrase beats "P@ss1!" — math the xkcd comic made famous.

quests.q: The attack where a hacker tries leaked username:password pairs from one breach against many other sites is called credential ______.
quests.hint: You "stuff" stolen creds into login forms en masse.
quests.explain: Credential stuffing works because people reuse passwords. Defenses: unique passwords, MFA, and breach-password checks. Try haveibeenpwned.

quests.q: Which free site lets you check if your email appeared in a known data breach? (name it — "have i been ____")
quests.hint: Hacker slang for "owned/defeated".
quests.explain: HaveIBeenPwned aggregates breach data. Checking your own accounts — and enabling its notifications — is a five-minute security upgrade.

quests.q: An attacker who sits between two parties silently relaying and altering messages is performing a ____-in-the-middle attack. One word.
quests.hint: M-I-T-M: ___-in-the-middle.
quests.explain: MITM intercepts traffic (rogue Wi-Fi, ARP spoofing). TLS + certificate validation is the countermeasure — which is why cert warnings matter.

quests.q: Segmenting a network so a breach in one zone can't reach others is called network ______. One word.
quests.hint: Dividing the network into segments/zones.
quests.explain: Flat networks let one foothold reach everything. Segmentation (VLANs, microsegmentation) is how you contain blast radius — a zero-trust pillar.

quests.q: Ransomware crews now steal data before encrypting, threatening to leak it — this two-pronged tactic is called ____ extortion. One word.
quests.hint: Two threats at once: encrypt AND leak.
quests.explain: Double extortion means backups alone won't save you — the data's already stolen. It reshaped ransomware defense toward prevention + DLP.

quests.q: Before clicking, you can reveal a link's true destination by doing what with your mouse (not clicking)?
quests.hint: Rest the cursor over it without pressing.
quests.explain: Hovering shows the real URL in the status bar — the simplest anti-phishing check there is. Displayed text can lie; the href cannot.

quests.q: Storing secrets like API keys in source code is dangerous; scanners look for them especially in ____ history even after deletion. One word.
quests.hint: Version-control history keeps deleted commits.
quests.explain: Deleting a key from the latest commit does NOT remove it from git history — it must be rotated. Secret scanning + pre-commit hooks prevent this.

quests.q: The security practice of encrypting data so a stolen laptop's drive is unreadable is called ______ at rest. One word.
quests.hint: Scrambling stored data.
quests.explain: Full-disk encryption (BitLocker/FileVault) makes a lost device a non-event instead of a breach. Turn it on — it's free and built in.

quests.q: OWASP's 2021 #1 web risk, where users can access data/actions they shouldn't, is broken ______ control. One word.
quests.hint: Who is allowed to do what.
quests.explain: Broken access control (e.g. changing ?id=123 to see another user's data) tops the OWASP Top 10. Enforce authz server-side, on every request.

quests.q: What does "RAG" stand for — retrieving documents to ground an LLM's answer?
quests.hint: R = retrieval, G = generation.
quests.explain: RAG fetches relevant context from a store and feeds it to the model, reducing hallucination and adding fresh knowledge.

quests.q: What 2024 open protocol lets LLMs connect to tools and data sources through a standard client-server interface?
quests.hint: Anthropic released it late 2024; abbreviated MCP.
quests.explain: MCP standardizes how models access tools/resources, so one server works across many AI clients — "USB-C for AI tools".

quests.q: The architecture behind modern LLMs, introduced in "Attention Is All You Need" (2017), is called the what?
quests.hint: Also a Hasbro toy line.
quests.explain: The Transformer replaced recurrence with self-attention, enabling parallel training at scale — the base of GPT, Claude, etc.

quests.q: What technique fine-tunes large models cheaply by training small low-rank adapter matrices instead of all weights?
quests.hint: Low-Rank Adaptation — a four-letter acronym.
quests.explain: LoRA freezes base weights and learns tiny rank-decomposed updates, cutting fine-tuning cost/memory by orders of magnitude.

quests.q: When an LLM confidently states something false, that's called a what?
quests.hint: A word normally about seeing things that aren't there.
quests.explain: Hallucination is fluent-but-wrong output. RAG, tool use, and citations reduce it; verification remains essential.

quests.q: What decoding parameter controls randomness by scaling logits before softmax — 0 = deterministic, high = creative?
quests.hint: A weather word.
quests.explain: Temperature scales the logits: low sharpens toward the top token (deterministic), high flattens the distribution (diverse).

quests.q: What are the numerical vector representations of text used for semantic search called?
quests.hint: They "embed" meaning into vectors.
quests.explain: Embeddings map text to vectors where distance ≈ semantic similarity — the backbone of RAG retrieval and clustering.

quests.q: Post-training alignment that learns from human preference rankings is abbreviated how?
quests.hint: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback.
quests.explain: RLHF trains a reward model on human preferences, then optimizes the policy against it — how chat models learn to be helpful/safe.

quests.q: An AI system that can take actions (call tools, browse, run code) in a loop toward a goal is called an AI what?
quests.hint: Like a secret ___ or travel ___.
quests.explain: An agent plans, acts via tools, observes results, and iterates. MCP + tool-use APIs are the current plumbing.

quests.q: What is the term for the maximum number of tokens a model can attend to at once?
quests.hint: Two words: surrounding text + an opening.
quests.explain: The context window bounds how much prompt+history the model sees. Frontier models now reach 100K–1M+ tokens.

quests.q: Models that handle text AND images (and sometimes audio/video) in one system are called what?
quests.hint: Multiple + modes.
quests.explain: Multimodal models fuse modalities (vision+language etc.), enabling image Q&A, chart reading, and document understanding.

quests.q: What image-generation model family denoises random noise step-by-step into an image?
quests.hint: It "spreads out" then reverses.
quests.explain: Diffusion models (Stable Diffusion, Imagen) learn to reverse a noising process, generating images from noise + a prompt.

quests.q: Giving a model a few worked examples in the prompt is called what kind of prompting?
quests.hint: A number of "shots" — more than zero, not many.
quests.explain: Few-shot prompting shows examples in-context so the model infers the pattern — no weight updates needed.

quests.q: The prompting technique "let's think step by step" that elicits intermediate reasoning is called what?
quests.hint: A chain made of reasoning steps.
quests.explain: Chain-of-thought prompts the model to show reasoning steps, improving accuracy on math/logic tasks.

quests.q: Reusing a pre-trained model on a new task with little data is called transfer what?
quests.hint: Transfer ___.
quests.explain: Transfer learning adapts general pretrained representations to specific tasks, slashing data/compute needs.

quests.q: What technique shrinks a model by training a small "student" to mimic a large "teacher"?
quests.hint: A chemistry word for purifying, applied to a student/teacher setup.
quests.explain: Distillation compresses a big model's behavior into a smaller, cheaper one that approximates its outputs.

quests.q: The unit an LLM reads and generates text in — often a word-piece — is called a what?
quests.hint: You also use these on a subway or in an arcade.
quests.explain: Tokens are sub-word chunks; billing, context limits, and speed are all measured in tokens.

quests.q: What is it called when a fine-tuned model forgets its original capabilities — "catastrophic ___"?
quests.hint: The opposite of remembering, and it's catastrophic.
quests.explain: Catastrophic forgetting: fine-tuning on new data erodes prior skills. Mitigations: replay, LoRA, regularization.

quests.q: A benchmark or test set used to measure model quality is generically called an what?
quests.hint: Short for "evaluation".
quests.explain: Evals quantify capability/safety on held-out tasks. Good evals are the difference between vibes and engineering.

quests.q: What phenomenon lets very large models suddenly perform tasks they weren't explicitly trained for, appearing at scale?
quests.hint: They "emerge" only past a size threshold.
quests.explain: Emergent abilities appear discontinuously with scale (though partly a metric artifact) — e.g. multi-step reasoning.

quests.q: What does an LLM predict at each step during generation?
quests.hint: The following unit of text.
quests.explain: Autoregressive LLMs predict the next token given all previous ones — repeated to produce full responses.

quests.q: The technique of forcing model output into a schema (e.g. valid JSON) is called what generation?
quests.hint: The opposite of free-form.
quests.explain: Structured/constrained generation guarantees parseable output (JSON, enums) via grammars or tool schemas — vital for agents.

quests.q: A vector database stores and searches over what?
quests.hint: The numeric meaning-vectors from earlier.
quests.explain: Vector DBs (Pinecone, pgvector, Qdrant) index embeddings for fast nearest-neighbor semantic search — the retrieval in RAG.

quests.q: What sampling method keeps the smallest set of top tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p?
quests.hint: Also called "top-p". The "nucleus" is that probability mass.
quests.explain: Nucleus (top-p) sampling truncates the tail dynamically, balancing diversity and coherence better than fixed top-k.

quests.q: The 2017 paper that introduced the Transformer has a famous four-word title: "Attention Is All You ____". Fill the blank.
quests.hint: Look up the paper — reading the source is the skill.
quests.explain: Reading primary sources beats summaries. This paper (Vaswani et al.) is 8 pages and underpins every modern LLM — worth an afternoon.

quests.q: A model with a 200,000-token context is fed a 150,000-token document. Roughly how many tokens of headroom remain for the answer? (number)
quests.hint: Context window minus input = room left for output. 200k − 150k.
quests.explain: Context budgeting is a daily engineering reality: input + output must fit the window. Misjudge it and generations get truncated.

quests.q: If 1 token ≈ 4 characters of English, roughly how many tokens is the 20-character string "machine learning ftw"? (number)
quests.hint: 20 characters ÷ 4 characters-per-token.
quests.explain: Estimating tokens (~¾ of a word each) lets you predict cost and fit before calling an API. Try a real tokenizer to calibrate.

quests.q: In attention, three learned projections of the input are the Query, the Key, and the ____. Fill the blank.
quests.hint: Q, K, and ___ — the trio of self-attention.
quests.explain: Attention scores queries against keys, then mixes values by those scores. Grasping Q/K/V is the gateway to understanding Transformers.

quests.q: What everyday tool would you use to check how a sentence splits into tokens before sending it to an LLM?
quests.hint: A "___izer" — it turns text into tokens.
quests.explain: A tokenizer visualizer shows exactly what the model sees. Surprise: numbers, emoji, and code often cost far more tokens than you'd guess.

quests.q: An agent loops: it reasons, then it ____, then observes the result, and repeats. The pattern (Reason+Act) is named what?
quests.hint: Reason + Act = the ____ pattern.
quests.explain: ReAct interleaves reasoning traces with tool calls, letting agents plan-act-observe. It's the mental model behind most tool-using agents.

quests.q: To make an LLM answer only from your company docs and cite them, you'd build a ____ pipeline (3-letter acronym).
quests.hint: Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
quests.explain: RAG is the default pattern for grounding models in private/fresh data without retraining. Build one — it's the most employable AI skill in 2025.

quests.q: Two text embeddings point almost the same direction. Their cosine similarity is close to which value — 1, 0, or −1?
quests.hint: Cosine similarity of identical directions is its maximum.
quests.explain: Cosine sim ranges −1…1; ~1 means near-identical meaning. This one number powers semantic search, dedup, and RAG ranking.

quests.q: Overfitting means a model memorized the ____ data and fails on new data. Fill the blank.
quests.hint: It learned the ___ set too well.
quests.explain: Overfitting = great on seen data, poor on unseen. Catch it by always holding out a validation/test set — the first rule of ML hygiene.

quests.q: A confusion-matrix metric: of all items the model flagged positive, the fraction actually positive is called what?
quests.hint: High when few false positives — contrast with recall.
quests.explain: Precision vs recall is the core tradeoff in classification (and RAG retrieval). Knowing which your task needs shapes the whole system.

quests.q: The "system prompt" of an assistant is used to set its ____ and rules before the user speaks. One word.
quests.hint: It defines how the model should act / its persona.
quests.explain: The system prompt is your steering wheel: role, tone, constraints, output format. Most "the model won't listen" bugs are weak system prompts.

quests.q: Running an open model like Llama on your own laptop with a tool such as Ollama is called ____ inference (as opposed to cloud). One word.
quests.hint: It runs on your own machine, not a remote API.
quests.explain: Local inference (Ollama, llama.cpp) gives privacy, zero per-token cost, and offline use — quantized models now run on a laptop. Try it.

quests.q: When you paste an image into a chat model and ask about it, you are using a ____ model (handles more than text). One word.
quests.hint: Multiple input modes: text AND images.
quests.explain: Multimodal models read charts, screenshots, and diagrams. A practical superpower: photograph a whiteboard and ask for the code.

quests.q: Quantizing a model to 4 bits mainly reduces its ____ footprint so it fits smaller hardware. One word (starts with m).
quests.hint: What fills up your GPU/RAM — smaller weights, less of it.
quests.explain: Quantization stores weights in fewer bits (e.g. 4-bit), shrinking memory ~4x with minor quality loss — how big models run on small GPUs.

quests.q: Prompt injection is the #1 risk on the OWASP Top 10 for ____ applications. Fill the blank (3 letters).
quests.hint: The OWASP list is specifically for ___ apps.
quests.explain: Before shipping any AI feature, read the OWASP LLM Top 10 once. Prompt injection topping it means: never trust model input as a command.

quests.q: Anthropic's open standard letting one tool server work across many AI clients is the Model Context ____. One word.
quests.hint: M-C-P: Model Context ___.
quests.explain: MCP is becoming the USB-C of AI tooling. Building one MCP server exposes your data to every compatible client — high-leverage to learn now.

quests.q: The practice of crafting and refining inputs to get better model outputs is called ____ engineering. One word.
quests.hint: You engineer the ___ you send the model.
quests.explain: Prompt engineering is the cheapest lever on quality — clear instructions, examples, and output format often beat a bigger model. Learn it first.

quests.q: Caching a long unchanging prefix (like a big system prompt) so repeat calls are cheaper/faster is called ____ caching. One word.
quests.hint: You cache the ___ so it isn't reprocessed each call.
quests.explain: Prompt caching reuses computation on a stable prefix, cutting cost and latency dramatically for agents with large fixed context. Know when it applies.

quests.q: When you let a model call your own functions (search, calculator, DB), that capability is called ____ use. One word.
quests.hint: Also known as "function calling".
quests.explain: Tool use turns a chat model into an agent that acts. Defining clean tool schemas is the difference between a demo and a reliable system.

quests.q: Using a strong LLM to grade another model's outputs at scale is the "LLM-as-a-____" evaluation pattern. One word.
quests.hint: The model acts as a ___ scoring answers.
quests.explain: LLM-as-judge scales evals beyond hand-grading, but needs careful rubrics and spot-checks against humans. Measuring quality is what separates pros.

quests.q: Splitting a long document into smaller pieces before embedding it for RAG is called ______. One word.
quests.hint: Breaking text into chunks.
quests.explain: Chunk size/overlap quietly makes or breaks RAG quality: too big buries the answer, too small loses context. Tuning it is a real, learnable skill.

quests.q: Feeding a model an image plus a question is possible because it is a ____-language model (VLM). One word.
quests.hint: V-L-M: ___-Language Model.
quests.explain: Vision-language models read screenshots, receipts, and diagrams. Pairing OCR-free image understanding with tools unlocks huge automation.

quests.q: Asking a model to "think step by step" to improve reasoning is called chain-of-______. One word.
quests.hint: Chain of ___ (CoT).
quests.explain: Chain-of-thought trades a few tokens for big accuracy gains on multi-step problems. Newer "reasoning" models do this internally — same principle.

quests.q: The failure where a model repeats the same phrase forever is a degenerate ______ loop, fixed partly by raising temperature or a repetition penalty. One word.
quests.hint: It keeps repeating — a ___ loop.
quests.explain: Repetition loops signal decoding/settings problems. Recognizing output pathologies (loops, cutoffs, refusals) and their knobs is practical debugging.

quests.q: The number that limits how many tokens a model may generate in one response is often called max ____ tokens. One word.
quests.hint: The cap on generated (output) length.
quests.explain: Set max output tokens too low and answers get cut mid-sentence; too high wastes budget. Matching it to the task is basic API craftsmanship.

quests.q: Fine-tuning only a few small added parameters instead of all weights is called ____-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). One word.
quests.hint: P-E-F-T: ___-Efficient Fine-Tuning.
quests.explain: PEFT (LoRA, adapters) makes customization affordable — train megabytes, not gigabytes. Knowing when to fine-tune vs just prompt/RAG saves months.

quests.q: An AI feature that can take real actions on your behalf should be tested for prompt ______ before launch. One word.
quests.hint: The #1 LLM security risk from earlier.
quests.explain: Any agent that reads untrusted text (web, email) can be hijacked by injected instructions. Threat-model it before shipping — treat model input as untrusted.

quests.q: Grounding answers in retrieved sources and showing them reduces hallucination and adds what the user can click to verify — ______. One word.
quests.hint: The clickable references backing each claim.
quests.explain: Citations make AI answers auditable and build trust. Designing systems that cite — and refuse when unsure — is the responsible-AI baseline.

quests.q: Ethereum scaling solutions that batch transactions off-chain and post proofs to L1 are called what (two words)?
quests.hint: L2. The layer above the base chain.
quests.explain: Layer-2 rollups (Arbitrum, Optimism, Base) execute off-chain and settle to Ethereum L1, cutting fees ~10–100x.

quests.q: What EIP, live since 2023, lets smart-contract wallets act as accounts — enabling gas sponsorship and social recovery?
quests.hint: ERC-4337 is the name of this concept.
quests.explain: Account abstraction (ERC-4337) makes wallets programmable: batched tx, paymasters, passkey login — no seed-phrase-only.

quests.q: What do you call the fee paid to execute a transaction on Ethereum?
quests.hint: It fuels the transaction.
quests.explain: Gas prices computation; fees = gas used × gas price. EIP-1559 split it into base fee (burned) + priority tip.

quests.q: Restaking protocols like EigenLayer let staked ETH secure additional services — those services are called what (acronym AVS)?
quests.hint: AVS — the middle word is "validated".
quests.explain: Restaking reuses ETH's economic security for AVSs (oracles, bridges, DA layers), earning extra yield at extra slashing risk.

quests.q: A cryptographic proof that reveals nothing except that a statement is true is a "zero-knowledge" what?
quests.explain: ZK proofs verify computation without revealing inputs — powering private tx and zk-rollups' validity proofs.

quests.q: What is the profit extracted by reordering/inserting transactions in a block, abbreviated MEV?
quests.hint: Formerly "miner", now "maximal", extractable value.
quests.explain: MEV is value captured by reordering/sandwiching tx (e.g. front-running DEX trades). PBS + fair-ordering aim to tame it.

quests.q: A token pegged 1:1 to a fiat currency like the US dollar is called a what?
quests.hint: It stays stable in price.
quests.explain: Stablecoins (USDC, USDT, DAI) hold a peg via reserves or crypto-collateral — the main medium of exchange on-chain.

quests.q: What 2024 narrative tokenizes physical/financial assets (treasuries, real estate) on-chain, abbreviated RWA?
quests.hint: RWA — the first three words.
quests.explain: RWA tokenization brings off-chain assets (T-bills, credit, property) on-chain for settlement/composability — BlackRock's BUIDL is a flagship.

quests.q: The recovery phrase for a self-custody wallet is typically how many words (most common)?
quests.hint: A dozen.
quests.explain: BIP-39 seed phrases are usually 12 or 24 words encoding the master key. Anyone with them owns the funds — never share.

quests.q: What DeFi mechanism lets you borrow and repay within a single transaction with no collateral, reverting if unpaid?
quests.hint: Fast as a camera ___.
quests.explain: Flash loans are atomic uncollateralized loans; if not repaid by tx end, everything reverts. Used for arbitrage — and exploits.

quests.q: A program that runs on a blockchain is called a smart what?
quests.hint: Smart ___.
quests.explain: Smart contracts are deployed code executed by the EVM; immutable once live, so bugs are costly — hence audits.

quests.q: What decentralized infrastructure narrative rewards people for providing real-world hardware (storage, wireless, compute), abbreviated DePIN?
quests.hint: DePIN — "Decentralized Physical Infrastructure Networks".
quests.explain: DePIN (Helium, Filecoin, Render) uses token incentives to bootstrap physical networks bottom-up instead of via a central company.

quests.q: The most widely used programming language for Ethereum smart contracts is what?
quests.hint: It sounds like the opposite of "liquidity".
quests.explain: Solidity is the dominant EVM contract language (curly-brace, statically typed). Vyper is the Pythonic alternative.

quests.q: What Ethereum upgrade (EIP-4844, 2024) added cheap temporary "blob" storage to slash L2 fees — nicknamed what?
quests.hint: Named after researchers Proto + Dankrad.
quests.explain: Proto-danksharding (EIP-4844) introduced blobs — cheap ephemeral data for rollups — dropping L2 costs dramatically.

quests.q: An NFT proves what about a digital item?
quests.hint: Who it belongs to.
quests.explain: NFTs are unique on-chain tokens proving ownership/provenance of an asset. The tech outlived the hype cycle for identity/tickets.

quests.q: What consensus mechanism did Ethereum switch to in "The Merge" (2022), replacing proof-of-work?
quests.hint: Validators "stake" ETH instead of burning electricity.
quests.explain: Proof-of-stake secures the chain via staked capital + slashing, cutting Ethereum's energy use ~99.95%.

quests.q: A "DAO" is a decentralized autonomous what?
quests.hint: Like a company, but on-chain and member-governed.
quests.explain: DAOs coordinate via on-chain governance tokens and treasuries — members vote on proposals instead of a boardroom.

quests.q: In an AMM DEX like Uniswap, what formula keeps the pool balanced — x times y equals what?
quests.hint: The constant-product formula: x*y = ___.
quests.explain: Constant-product AMMs hold x·y=k; trades move price along the curve. Enables permissionless liquidity without order books.

quests.q: Bridging tokens between two blockchains uses a piece of infrastructure called a what?
quests.hint: It connects two sides.
quests.explain: Bridges move assets across chains by lock-and-mint or burn-and-release. Historically the biggest hack target in crypto.

quests.q: The 2022 Ronin bridge hack ($625M) succeeded by compromising a majority of what?
quests.hint: The attacker controlled enough signing keys to approve withdrawals.
quests.explain: Ronin used 9 validators; the attacker got 5 keys and forged withdrawals. Lesson: decentralize signers, monitor thresholds.

quests.q: The wallet browser extension most associated with Ethereum is called what?
quests.hint: A fox logo; "meta" + a face covering.
quests.explain: MetaMask is the dominant EVM browser wallet. Always verify the tx details it shows before signing — signatures are irreversible.

quests.q: What attack drains a wallet by tricking a user into signing a malicious token-approval or "permit" message?
quests.hint: It abuses ERC-20 "approve"/"permit" signatures.
quests.explain: Approval phishing gets a victim to sign an unlimited token allowance or Permit2 message; the attacker then transfers funds. Revoke unused approvals.

quests.q: Gas fees on Ethereum are denominated in a tiny unit of ETH called what?
quests.hint: Rhymes with "way"; billionth of an ETH.
quests.explain: 1 gwei = 10⁻⁹ ETH. Gas prices are quoted in gwei; wallets estimate total fee from gas × gwei.

quests.q: What property lets DeFi protocols stack like Lego because they share standards and can call each other?
quests.hint: Things "compose" together.
quests.explain: Composability ("money legos") lets contracts freely integrate — a strength for innovation and a systemic-risk multiplier.

quests.q: An Ethereum address is 40 hex characters long and starts with which two-character prefix?
quests.hint: Every hex value in Ethereum starts with this.
quests.explain: Recognizing 0x… addresses and hashes is table stakes. Learning to read an address vs a tx hash vs a contract prevents costly mistakes.

quests.q: Paste any tx hash into which website to inspect it publicly on Ethereum mainnet? (the block explorer, one word .io/.com)
quests.hint: The famous Ethereum block ___.
quests.explain: Block explorers make chains auditable by anyone. Reading a transaction on Etherscan — from, to, value, logs — is the core web3 literacy skill.

quests.q: 1 ether = 10 to the power of how many wei? (the smallest unit) — give the exponent.
quests.hint: A quintillion wei per ether.
quests.explain: 1 ETH = 10¹⁸ wei. Off-by-a-few-decimals errors here have cost people fortunes. On-chain math is unforgiving — always mind the units.

quests.q: The ERC standard for fungible tokens (the interface almost every token implements) is ERC-____. Number.
quests.hint: The original token standard number.
quests.explain: ERC-20 defines transfer/approve/balanceOf. Reading a standard's interface tells you exactly what a contract can do — start with this one.

quests.q: The standard for NFTs (non-fungible tokens) is ERC-____. Number.
quests.hint: The classic NFT standard.
quests.explain: ERC-721 gives each token a unique id + owner. ERC-1155 came later for mixed fungible/NFT batches. Knowing which is which reads any collection.

quests.q: In Solidity, a function marked ____ can receive ETH. Fill the keyword.
quests.hint: Without this keyword, sending ETH to the function reverts.
quests.explain: The payable keyword is a classic gotcha: forget it and deposits fail. Reading Solidity modifiers (view/pure/payable) reveals what a contract does.

quests.q: Before signing a transaction, the one thing you must always check in your wallet popup is the ____ address (where funds go). One word.
quests.hint: The "to" / destination — who receives it.
quests.explain: Address-poisoning scams plant lookalike addresses hoping you copy the wrong one. Verifying the recipient every time is the habit that saves wallets.

quests.q: A tool like revoke.cash lets you see and cancel your token ____ granted to contracts. One word.
quests.hint: The "approve" permissions you signed earlier.
quests.explain: Old unlimited approvals are a standing liability — a later exploit of that contract can drain you. Auditing/revoking approvals is basic hygiene.

quests.q: A stablecoin aims to hold a value of about how many US dollars? Number.
quests.hint: Pegged one-to-one to the dollar.
quests.explain: When a "stable"coin drifts from $1 (depeg), something is wrong with its backing. Watching the peg is how you gauge stablecoin health.

quests.q: The 2022 collapse of the UST algorithmic stablecoin and its sister token wiped out ~$40B. Name the sister/LUNA project (one word).
quests.hint: LUNA was the token of the ___ ecosystem.
quests.explain: Terra/UST showed algorithmic pegs can death-spiral. Studying failures (Terra, FTX, bridges) teaches risk faster than any bull-market thread.

quests.q: Never share your wallet's 12- or 24-word recovery phrase, also called the ____ phrase. One word.
quests.hint: The words that regenerate your whole wallet.
quests.explain: Anyone with your seed phrase owns your funds — permanently, irreversibly. No legitimate support agent ever needs it. This rule has no exceptions.

quests.q: "Not your keys, not your ____." Complete the famous self-custody saying (one word).
quests.hint: If you don't hold the keys, you don't truly hold the…
quests.explain: Assets on an exchange are IOUs — FTX proved it. Self-custody means holding your own keys. The tradeoff: total control, total responsibility.

quests.q: A gas fee that spikes during network congestion is measured in gwei, which is a unit of ____. One word.
quests.hint: Gwei is a denomination of ETH itself.
quests.explain: Fees rise with demand for blockspace. Checking a gas tracker before transacting — and batching or waiting — is a simple money-saving skill.

quests.q: Zero-knowledge rollups post a validity ____ to L1 to prove their off-chain transactions were correct. One word.
quests.hint: ZK = zero-knowledge ___.
quests.explain: ZK-rollups inherit L1 security by posting succinct validity proofs — no need to trust the operator. This is where scaling + privacy converge.

quests.q: DeFi lending protocols require borrowers to post ____ worth more than they borrow (over-______). One word.
quests.hint: The asset you lock up to back a loan.
quests.explain: Overcollateralization is why most DeFi loans need no credit check — the protocol can liquidate you if your collateral drops. Understand liquidation before you borrow.

quests.q: A flash loan borrows and repays within a single ____, reverting entirely if unpaid. One word.
quests.hint: Atomic: it all happens in one on-chain ___.
quests.explain: Flash loans exploit atomicity — huge uncollateralized capital for one transaction. Studying how they power arbitrage AND exploits sharpens system thinking.

quests.q: The #1 rule when a DM offers "free airdrop, connect wallet here" is to do what? (one word — the action you should NOT take, e.g. "don't ____")
quests.hint: Never ___ your wallet to random sites from DMs.
quests.explain: Wallet-drainer scams live in DMs and fake airdrops. Never connect or sign on sites you didn't seek out. Skepticism is your best on-chain security tool.

quests.q: A smart-contract bug where an external call re-enters the function before state updates is the ______ attack that drained The DAO in 2016. One word.
quests.hint: The call "re-enters" mid-execution.
quests.explain: Reentrancy (The DAO, $60M) is the most famous Solidity bug. The fix — checks-effects-interactions — is now dogma. Study it to think like an auditor.

quests.q: An audit is a professional ______ review of a smart contract before it handles real money. One word.
quests.hint: They review it for ___ flaws.
quests.explain: Unaudited contracts holding funds are gambling. Learning to read an audit report — scope, findings, severity — tells you what a protocol's risk really is.

quests.q: The mechanism that automatically sells a borrower's collateral when it falls below a threshold is called ______. One word.
quests.hint: Your position gets ___ed if collateral drops too far.
quests.explain: Liquidation protects lenders but can cascade in a crash. Understanding health factors and liquidation thresholds is essential before touching DeFi leverage.

quests.q: Impermanent loss is a risk faced by people who provide ______ to an AMM pool. One word.
quests.hint: Liquidity providers (LPs) supply this to the pool.
quests.explain: Impermanent loss means an LP can end up worse than just holding. Knowing this before farming "high APY" pools separates informed from rekt.

quests.q: On-chain, a smart contract that feeds external real-world data (like ETH price) to other contracts is called an ______. One word.
quests.hint: It "speaks" outside data onto the chain.
quests.explain: Oracles (Chainlink) bridge off-chain data on-chain; manipulating a weak price oracle is a classic exploit vector. Every DeFi risk model starts here.

quests.q: Governance tokens let holders ____ on protocol proposals. One word.
quests.hint: One token, one ___ (roughly).
quests.explain: Token governance decides upgrades and treasury spend. Reading active proposals on a protocol's forum shows you where power and money actually flow.

quests.q: A "rug pull" is when a project's team suddenly removes ______ and disappears with investors' funds. One word.
quests.hint: They pull the ___ out from under the token.
quests.explain: Rug pulls exploit trust and locked-liquidity claims. Checking whether liquidity is locked/renounced is a basic due-diligence habit that avoids disasters.

quests.q: Layer-2 networks exist mainly to make transactions ______ (lower fees) than Ethereum mainnet. One word.
quests.hint: The opposite of expensive.
quests.explain: L2s (Base, Arbitrum, Optimism) cut fees by orders of magnitude while inheriting L1 security. Knowing which L2 an app uses shapes your cost and risk.

quests.q: The site L2BEAT is the go-to place to compare the security and TVL of Ethereum ______ solutions. One word.
quests.hint: It rates ___ (L2) solutions.
quests.explain: L2BEAT independently rates rollups on real security assumptions, not marketing. Using neutral data sources over project claims is core web3 literacy.

quests.q: Before aping into a token, checking its ______ (total value locked or market cap) gives a basic sense of scale. One word.
quests.hint: Total Value Locked — three letters.
quests.explain: TVL and volume are quick health signals; tiny illiquid tokens are easy to manipulate. Building the habit of checking data first prevents FOMO losses.

quests.q: DeFiLlama is a neutral aggregator best known for tracking ______ across every DeFi protocol. Three-letter metric.
quests.hint: The same Total Value Locked metric.
quests.explain: DeFiLlama gives unbiased, cross-protocol TVL and yields. Learning to read aggregators instead of trusting any single project's dashboard is a durable skill.
